**Slides (PDF):** [week03-cost-revenue.pdf](slides/week03-cost-revenue.pdf)

Week 2 asked **who competes** and why scarce pads and density matter for average cost. This week asks whether the **numbers** work: investment vs operating cost, the right unit, breakeven volume, how revenue models reshape who bears usage risk, and how weather downtime hits cash flow.

**Orient refreshers:**

- [Glossary · CASK / CAPEX / OPEX](glossary.qmd#business-and-economics) — definitions used below  
- [How does LAE work?](business-overview.qmd) — roles that own different cost lines  
- [Week 2](week-02.qmd) — density, ATC, and scarce sites that feed this week's unit costs  

## Summary {#summary}

**Before you go**

- How to separate CAPEX, fixed OPEX, and activity-related variable cost.
- Unit-cost measures you will use: [CASK](glossary.qmd#business-and-economics) and cost per mission-kilometre.
- Breakeven volume and how price, load factor, and utilization move the numbers.
- Revenue-model choices (pay-per-use, subscription, availability, complementary) and weather as a planning risk.

**Takeaways**

- Always separate CAPEX, recurring fixed OPEX, and variable cost before talking about unit economics.
- CASK is about passenger capacity offered; cargo and public-service work often need mission-based measures.
- Breakeven needs a consistent unit, contribution margin, realistic capacity, and realistic demand.
- Revenue management aims to improve total contribution—not just fill every seat.
- Subscriptions and similar contracts can reshape risk; none is a free or guaranteed hedge.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Classroom numbers vs absolute facts.** Worked examples below use round figures (asset costs, CASK, fares, missions, weather days). They are **illustrative assumptions for learning**, not current Hong Kong market quotations, operator filings, or forecasts. Absolute programme and reading facts (first Sandbox **38 of 72**, Sandbox X ≠ first Sandbox, NASA UAM study as **not** an HK government figure, CAAC delivery-trial guide as a comparator cost-line document) stay with issuers on [Key numbers](key-figures.qmd) / [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats) / [Readings](#readings).
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of Week 3 you should be able to:

1. **Distinguish** CAPEX from OPEX in an LAE business model, and separate recurring fixed OPEX from activity-related variable cost.  
2. **Calculate** simple unit-cost measures, including [CASK](glossary.qmd#business-and-economics) and cost per mission-kilometre.  
3. **Estimate** breakeven volume and explain how price, load factor, and utilization affect viability.  
4. **Compare** pay-per-use, subscription, availability-based, and complementary revenue models.  
5. **Evaluate** how weather downtime and cost differences across Hong Kong and the GBA affect strategy — without treating any hedge as free or guaranteed.

## 1. Why cost and revenue structure come next

A technically feasible LAE service is not automatically commercially viable. Managers must connect **asset cost**, **daily operations**, **capacity**, **demand**, **pricing**, and **risk**.

Imagine two reviews of the same business case. One manager asks how charging time, maintenance, and turnaround cap daily missions. Another asks whether subscriptions or availability contracts could make revenue more predictable. Both questions sit inside this week's toolkit.

### Link back to Week 2

Week 2 showed that scarce pads and density drive **average total cost (ATC)**. Week 3 makes that precise for a spreadsheet: what is **investment**, what is **recurring spend**, what is the right **unit**, and how does the **revenue model** change who bears volume risk? The same pad that raised ATC when under-used now appears as CAPEX or site OPEX; the same density logic reappears as utilization in CASK and as missions in breakeven.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Sandbox note.** Trial programmes (first **Regulatory Sandbox**, **38 of 72** selected; later **Sandbox X**) generate learning and, for some operators, real compliance and insurance OPEX. They are **not** a cost forecast or a proof that commercial unit economics already work. Keep programmes separate ([Key numbers](key-figures.qmd); [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats)).
:::

Section 1 placed cost and revenue after market structure. Start with the **cost stack**. Ask three questions: what is capital, what recurs every day, and how those pieces become a rough daily economic cost.

## 2. CAPEX, OPEX, and a daily economic-cost sketch

### CAPEX vs OPEX

**CAPEX** is capital expenditure (money spent up front on assets). **OPEX** is operating expenditure (money spent to keep running). Keep them separate before you build any unit-cost number.

| Label | Plain meaning | Typical LAE examples |
|-------|---------------|----------------------|
| [**CAPEX**](glossary.qmd#capex-opex) (capital expenditure) | Investment in assets that provide benefits over several years | Aircraft, charging equipment, vertiport construction, major software platforms |
| [**OPEX**](glossary.qmd#capex-opex) (operating expenditure) | Recurring spend to operate the service | Energy, maintenance, staff, insurance, site fees, communications, routine compliance |

**Important nuance:** certification and approval expenditure is **not automatically CAPEX**. Accounting treatment depends on the nature of the spend and applicable rules. For managerial classroom work, keep a separate line for compliance / approval cash so you do not bury it inside “aircraft” or “OPEX” without thought.

Also separate, inside OPEX:

- **Recurring fixed OPEX** — paid even at zero missions that day (many site fees, base staff, insurance).  
- **Variable (activity-related) cost** — rises with missions or flight hours (energy, wear, some labour).

Glossary: [CAPEX / OPEX](glossary.qmd#business-and-economics).

**Connecting idea.** The CAPEX / OPEX label answers an *accounting and cash-timing* question. The fixed / variable split answers a *managerial* question: what still burns cash if the fleet sits on the ground? Weather and demand shocks make that split non-negotiable. Mixing the two axes (“CAPEX is fixed, OPEX is variable”) is a common error — major software platforms can be CAPEX, and energy is OPEX but largely variable.

### A simple daily economic-cost approximation

In words: take net asset cost (purchase price minus expected residual), spread it over useful operating days, then add that day's operating spend.

$$
\text{Daily economic cost}
=
\frac{\text{Asset cost} - \text{Expected residual value}}{\text{Useful operating days}}
+ \text{Daily OPEX}
$$

This spreads net asset cost across expected operating life and adds daily operating spend. Financing cost, maintenance cycles, downtime, and residual value may need separate treatment in a full model. Treat the formula as an **economic-cost sketch**, not complete accounting depreciation or a full cash-flow statement.

### Worked illustration (investment level and unit cost)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** five-year life; no residual value; useful days $= 5 \times 365 = 1{,}825$; daily OPEX = HK$8,000; **50 missions** per operating day.

| | Case A: HK$10M investment | Case B: HK$6M investment |
|--|----------------------------|---------------------------|
| Daily asset allocation | $10\text{M}/1{,}825 \approx$ **HK$5,479** | $6\text{M}/1{,}825 \approx$ **HK$3,288** |
| + Daily OPEX | HK$8,000 | HK$8,000 |
| Total daily economic cost | HK$13,479 | HK$11,288 |
| **Cost per mission** | $\approx$ **HK$270** | $\approx$ **HK$226** |

**Takeaway:** higher investment raises unit cost, but utilization and operating cost remain equally important. Cutting missions from 50 to 25 would roughly double cost per mission even if investment stayed at Case B — the Week 2 density lesson in different clothes.

### The “Hong Kong premium” as a hypothesis

Why might an LAE service cost more to operate in Hong Kong? Class lists **hypotheses to test**, not proven universal mark-ups:

- Scarce sites, structural works, charging, passenger access, and safety facilities.  
- Dense buildings, terrain, communications, weather, and interactions with other airspace users.  
- Skilled labour and professional services (engineering, insurance, legal, compliance).  
- Reliability requirements (redundancy, maintenance capability, contingency planning).

The size of any premium depends on application, site, and operating model. Compare specific cases — do not paste a single “HK multiplier” into every spreadsheet.

---

CAPEX, OPEX, and a daily cost sketch answer “what does it take to stand ready?” Unit economics asks the next question: **cost and revenue per meaningful unit of activity**.

Before naming CASK, lock the **stack**:

1. List CAPEX items and an economic-life assumption.  
2. Split OPEX into recurring fixed vs activity-related.  
3. Choose the **unit** that matches the product (seat-km for passenger capacity offered; mission-km or mission for cargo / public service).  
4. Only then compute a unit cost and ask whether revenue per unit covers contribution.

That order prevents the classic mistake of computing a polished CASK from a muddled cost base.

| Question | Tool this week | Week 2 cousin |
|----------|----------------|---------------|
| What did we buy? | CAPEX / residual / useful days | Sunk site cost |
| What burns if we fly zero? | Fixed OPEX | Fixed cost in ATC |
| What rises with each mission? | Variable cost | Marginal cost |
| Cost of capacity offered? | CASK | ATC at a given utilization |
| How many units to survive? | Breakeven / required missions | Density needed to lower ATC |

---

The tool chain maps stack → unit measures → breakeven. [**CASK**](glossary.qmd#cask-cpmk) (cost per available seat-kilometre) and mission-kilometres are two classroom unit metrics — choose the unit that matches the service, not the buzzword.

## 4. Unit economics: CASK and mission-kilometres

**Unit economics** studies revenue and cost for **one** meaningful unit of activity (one flight, one seat-kilometre, one mission):

- Passenger service — per flight, available seat-kilometre, or paying passenger-trip.  
- Cargo or public-service work — per mission, mission-kilometre, or kilogram delivered.

### CASK (cost per available seat-kilometre)

In words: take operating cost for the period and divide by the seat-kilometres of capacity you **offered** (seats × kilometres flown), whether sold or empty.

$$
CASK = \frac{\text{Operating cost for the period}}{\text{Available seats} \times \text{Kilometres flown}}
$$

Available seat-kilometres measure **capacity offered**, whether seats are sold or not. More productive use can spread some fixed operating costs over more seat-km. A low CASK does **not** guarantee profit: the operator must still fill seats and earn enough revenue. Turnaround, charging, maintenance, weather, route length, and capacity all affect the measure.

Glossary: [CASK / CPMK](glossary.qmd#business-and-economics).

**Connecting idea.** CASK is a **cost-of-capacity** metric. It does not replace revenue per passenger, contribution margin, or cash flow. Airlines sometimes pair cost and yield ideas; in this course, keep the managerial order clear: (1) what does capacity cost, (2) what contribution does a sold seat or mission earn, (3) how many units cover fixed cost. Do not invent Hong Kong eVTOL CASK benchmarks from airline averages — the cost stack and mission profile differ.

### Worked illustration (utilization and CASK)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** four available seats; operating cost **HK$12,000/day**; each trip **10 km**.

| | 10 trips/day | 50 trips/day |
|--|--------------|--------------|
| Available seat-km | $4 \times 10 \times 10 = 400$ | $4 \times 50 \times 10 = 2{,}000$ |
| **CASK** | $12{,}000/400 =$ **HK$30** per seat-km | $12{,}000/2{,}000 =$ **HK$6** per seat-km |
| Allocated cost of one seat on a 10 km trip | HK$300 | HK$60 |

Higher utilization lowers CASK in this simplified example; it still does not prove demand or profitability. If charging and pad turnaround cannot support 50 trips, the right-hand column is fiction — Week 2 capacity limits return here.

### Cost per mission-kilometre

For cargo, inspection, emergency, or public-service missions:

$$
\text{Cost per mission-km}
=
\frac{\text{Operating cost for the period}}{\text{Total mission-kilometres}}
$$

Longer missions create more mission-km mechanically — compare routes with attention to length, payload, quality, and complexity.

**Assumptions (illustrative):** daily operating cost HK$12,000; average mission **8 km**.

| | 20 missions/day | 100 missions/day |
|--|-----------------|------------------|
| Mission-km | 160 | 800 |
| Cost per mission-km | HK$75 | HK$15 |
| Allocated cost per mission | **HK$600** | **HK$120** |

Volume can cut allocated unit cost; capacity, demand, turnaround, and service rules constrain how much volume you can actually run (Week 2 density logic returns here).

---

Unit cost alone does not pay the bills. **Revenue models** decide who pays for readiness vs usage — and who bears empty-seat or grounded-day risk.

## 5. Revenue models: more than one transaction type

LAE businesses may combine several models:

| Model | Revenue predictability (typical) | Who bears usage risk (typical) | Possible use |
|-------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------|--------------|
| **Pay per use** | Lower | Operator | Passenger trip, delivery, inspection |
| **Subscription / membership** | Medium | Shared | Frequent users; priority or allowance |
| **Availability-based contract** | Higher | Customer / shared | Public or critical readiness |
| **Complementary services** | Varies | Varies | Data, analytics, maintenance, platform |

Match the model to the **value promised** and the party best able to manage the risk. A subscription is not guaranteed cash unless customers accept terms and keep paying. Data does not monetise itself — it needs useful products, rights, demand, security, and privacy compliance. Mixing models can diversify revenue but raises contractual and operational complexity. Week 6 returns to partnerships and payment designs.

**Connecting idea.** Availability payments buy **readiness**, not necessarily high flight volume. That is attractive when public agencies value coverage on bad weather days — and expensive for the buyer if paid capacity sits idle. Pay-per-use looks “simple” until a multi-day storm zeros usage revenue while fixed OPEX continues (Session 3). Choose the model for the **risk you can actually manage**, not for the label that sounds modern.

A revenue model names the transaction. [**Revenue management**](glossary.qmd#revenue-management) allocates scarce seats, slots, or payload toward contribution — not toward filling every seat at any price.

## 6. Revenue management (not “fill every seat”)

**Revenue management** allocates limited capacity and adjusts prices or conditions to improve **total expected contribution** — not merely to eliminate empty seats.

- Selling too cheaply can fill capacity while destroying revenue.  
- Holding capacity for later high-value demand can sometimes raise total contribution.  
- Managers weigh price, booking time, segment, expected demand, cancellations, and capacity.

**Managerial objective:** sell the right capacity to the right customer at the right time and price.

A simple passenger-revenue identity — in words, seats offered times the share occupied by paying passengers times the average fare they pay:

$$
\text{Revenue per flight}
=
\text{Seats} \times \text{Load factor} \times \text{Average fare}
$$

Load factor is the share of available seats occupied by **paying** passengers. Average fare should reflect discounts and mix. Maximising load factor alone is the wrong goal if fares collapse.

**Connecting idea.** Load factor links **CASK** (cost of seats offered) to **cash** (seats sold). High utilization that fills seats at wrecked fares can look good on a load-factor chart and still fail contribution. For cargo, replace “load factor × fare” with payload × price per kg or price per mission — same managerial idea, different unit.

---

Pricing and mix improve contribution *given* volume. [**Breakeven**](glossary.qmd#breakeven-volume) asks how much volume you need before fixed cost is covered — and whether that volume is physically feasible.

## 7. Breakeven volume

For one consistent service unit (flight, passenger, delivery, or mission):

$$
\text{Breakeven units}
=
\frac{\text{Fixed cost}}{\text{Revenue per unit} - \text{Variable cost per unit}}
$$

The denominator is **contribution margin per unit**. For passenger flights, revenue per flight depends on fare **and** paying passengers per flight.

Equivalently, a daily activity target:

$$
\text{Required missions per day}
=
\frac{\text{Fixed daily cost}}{\text{Contribution margin per mission}}
$$

Compare that target with physical capacity, operating hours, charging, maintenance, weather, and expected demand. This required-activity number is **not** the usual statistical “utilization rate” (actual use ÷ available capacity or time). Revenue management can improve contribution; it cannot invent unlimited capacity or demand.

```{=html}
<figure class="wdiag wdiag-svg" id="w03-breakeven-svg" aria-labelledby="w03-breakeven-svg-title">
<p class="wdiag-cap" id="w03-breakeven-svg-title"><strong>Breakeven volume</strong> — breakeven units = fixed cost ÷ (revenue per unit − variable cost per unit). Denominator = <strong>contribution margin</strong> per unit. Daily form: required missions/day = fixed daily cost ÷ contribution margin per mission. Compare with capacity, hours, charging, weather, and demand — required activity is <strong>not</strong> an automatic traffic forecast. Classroom units only.</p>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 720 340" role="img" style="display:block;width:100%;max-width:44rem;height:auto;margin:.35rem 0 .15rem" aria-labelledby="j1-title j1-desc">
  <title id="j1-title">Breakeven volume</title>
  <desc id="j1-desc">Breakeven units equal fixed cost divided by contribution margin per unit, where contribution margin is revenue per unit minus variable cost per unit. Equivalently, required missions per day equal fixed daily cost divided by contribution margin per mission. Compare the target with physical capacity, hours, charging, weather and expected demand. Classroom units only.</desc>
```

### Worked illustration (price and breakeven)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** fixed cost **HK$20,000/day**; variable cost **HK$100 per mission**.

| Revenue per mission | Contribution | Breakeven missions/day |
|---------------------|--------------|-------------------------|
| HK$500 | HK$400 | $20{,}000/400 =$ **50** |
| HK$200 | HK$100 | $20{,}000/100 =$ **200** |

Discounting sharply raises required volume — test whether that volume fits capacity and demand.

### Worked illustration (load factor and breakeven flights)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** four seats; average fare HK$500; fixed cost HK$20,000/day; variable cost HK$100/**flight**.

Fractional passengers are averages across many flights. Higher load factor can cut required flights **if** fare and costs stay unchanged.

### Sensitivity habit (classroom method)

Class exercises often shock one input at a time — for example higher site rent, or several grounded days — then ask how much price or utilization must rise to restore breakeven. That habit matters more than any single template:

1. Freeze a transparent base case (fixed, variable, price, capacity).  
2. Shock **one** driver (rent, energy, downtime, fare).  
3. Recompute contribution and required activity.  
4. Ask whether the new target is physically and commercially feasible.

Do not treat an in-class “airport shuttle” spreadsheet as a real Hong Kong operator model; it is a teaching dashboard for shocks.

---

Breakeven on a clear-weather day is incomplete. **Weather downtime** hits revenue, fixed OPEX, and sometimes contracts at once — so risk responses belong in the same workbook as CASK.

## 8. Weather downtime and risk responses

Severe weather can hit an LAE business through several channels at once:

- lost trips and revenue;  
- continued aircraft, site, staff, insurance, and financing costs;  
- disruption, refunds, and service-level penalties;  
- repositioning, inspection, maintenance, and recovery costs;  
- lower willingness to rely on the service next time.

A weather warning does not mechanically ground every operation; restrictions depend on aircraft capability, location, approval, and conditions.

### Managing weather risk

Combine operational, contractual, and financial tools:

- **Operational resilience** — forecasting, spare capacity, alternative modes/routes, recovery plans.  
- **Contract design** — availability payments, minimum commitments, cancellation terms, service credits, force majeure.  
- **Insurance or parametric cover** — possible payout on an agreed trigger, subject to exclusions, basis risk, and premium.  
- **Liquidity** — cash or committed financing for temporary shortfalls.

Subscriptions and reservation fees transfer risk **only if** customers accept the terms and see real value. None of these tools is a free hedge.

**Connecting idea.** Hong Kong policy language has noted industry work on LAE insurance products that draw on Regulatory Sandbox data ([Glossary](glossary.qmd) / Policy Address citations there). That is evidence that **insurance product design is an active theme** — not evidence that any named operator already has cheap parametric cover, nor that Sandbox participation equals commercial insurance readiness. Treat premiums, exclusions, and basis risk as first-class model inputs when you claim a hedge.

### Profit under a mixed-revenue sketch

In words: add committed, usage, and any insurance cash; subtract fixed and variable operating cost plus premiums and service credits.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Profit} ={}& \text{Committed revenue} + \text{Usage revenue} + \text{Insurance payout} \\
&- \text{Fixed cost} - \text{Variable cost} - \text{Premiums and service credits}
\end{aligned}
$$

Committed revenue can reduce exposure to flight volume but usually adds availability obligations. Downtime may save some variable cost while still creating refunds, credits, recovery costs, or reputational damage. The aim is manageable cash flow and service obligations — not to “profit from storms.”

### Worked illustration (five grounded days)

**Assumptions (illustrative):** 30-day month; **25** operating days; 50 missions/day on open days; usage revenue HK$500/mission; fixed cost HK$600,000/month; variable cost HK$100/mission. Missions $= 25 \times 50 = 1{,}250$.

| | Pay per mission only | Committed monthly revenue HK$750,000 |
|--|----------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Usage / contract revenue | HK$625,000 | HK$750,000 |
| Variable cost | HK$125,000 | HK$125,000 |
| Fixed cost | HK$600,000 | HK$600,000 |
| **Result (before credits/premiums)** | **Loss HK$100,000** | **Profit HK$25,000** |

Committed revenue may stabilise cash flow; the contract must still specify availability, refunds, credits, and weather obligations. Illustration excludes taxes, financing, premiums, recovery costs, and possible service credits.

Cost and revenue tools are general. **Hong Kong and GBA hypotheses** ask which cost lines and revenue mixes are plausible locally — without pasting foreign TAM figures into a local case.

## 9. Hong Kong and the GBA: cost and revenue hypotheses

| Dimension | Hong Kong possibility | Wider GBA possibility |
|-----------|----------------------|------------------------|
| Site environment | Dense and constrained | More varied |
| Customer base | Premium and specialised | Larger and more diverse |
| Cost pressure | Site and professional costs | Varies by city and use case |
| Scale opportunity | Complex urban services | Manufacturing and network scale |
| Potential role | Finance, logistics, services | Technology, production, operations |

These are **strategic hypotheses**, not universal facts. Compare specific sites, routes, customers, regulations, and partners. Keep trial programmes straight: **Regulatory Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**; neither is a cost or revenue forecast ([Who decides what?](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats); [Key numbers](key-figures.qmd)).

Compliance and trial rules can become real OPEX lines — for example Mainland delivery-trial guidance listed in [Readings](#readings) turns record-keeping, insurance, and link requirements into operating-cost items for operators who face those rules (comparator context, **not** Hong Kong Cap. 448G text).

**Connecting idea.** When you cite the NASA *Urban Air Mobility Market Study* ([Readings](#readings)), use it as **official UAM framing and constraint thinking** (legal, weather, infrastructure, acceptance shrink unconstrained markets). Do **not** paste its dollar or TAM figures into a Hong Kong business case as if they were local forecasts, and do not treat NASA as Hong Kong law or as an HKSAR government number.

Hypotheses need a sequence. The **one-page tool map** walks investment → unit cost → revenue → breakeven → capacity consistency so the spreadsheet cannot silently contradict itself.

## 10. One-page tool map (from investment to cash)

| Step | Ask | Output |
|------|-----|--------|
| 1 | What assets and life? | Daily asset allocation |
| 2 | What fixed vs variable OPEX? | Cost stack |
| 3 | What unit matches the product? | Seat-km or mission-km / mission |
| 4 | What is unit cost at realistic utilization? | CASK or cost per mission |
| 5 | What is revenue and contribution per unit? | Fare × load (or mission price − variable) |
| 6 | How many units cover fixed cost? | Breakeven / required daily activity |
| 7 | Who bears volume risk? | Pay-per-use vs subscription vs availability |
| 8 | What if weather cuts open days? | Mixed-revenue profit + hedge costs |

If step 6’s required activity exceeds step 4’s physical capacity, the model is inconsistent — fix price, cost, capacity, or the product before defending the case.

If step 6 required activity exceeds step 4 physical capacity, the model is <strong>inconsistent</strong> — fix price, cost, capacity, or product.</p>

Pull the thread. Build the cost stack. Choose unit metrics. Design revenue. Apply revenue management. Check breakeven under downtime. State place-specific hypotheses. Then refuse sandbox participation as proof of unit economics.

## 11. Putting Week 3 together

- Separate **CAPEX**, recurring **fixed OPEX**, and **variable** cost before any unit metric. Use **CASK** for passenger capacity offered and **mission-based** measures for cargo / public service.
- Breakeven needs a **consistent unit**, contribution margin, and a check against capacity and demand. Revenue management maximises **contribution**, not empty-seat guilt.
- Subscriptions, availability contracts, insurance, and liquidity **reshape** risk — none is a free guarantee. Sandbox learning and compliance lines are real in cash, not substitutes for unit economics.

Short checklist: [Summary](#summary).

---

### Study checklist {#study-checklist}

1. Separate **CAPEX**, recurring **fixed OPEX**, and **variable** cost on one page before any unit metric.  
2. Explain why certification cash is **not automatically CAPEX**.  
3. Compute the **daily economic-cost** sketch and cost per mission under two investment levels.  
4. State the **Hong Kong premium** only as hypotheses to test — never as a universal multiplier.  
5. Compute **CASK** at low and high utilization; say what CASK does **not** prove.  
6. Compute **cost per mission-km** and explain why longer routes can mislead comparisons.  
7. Compare four **revenue models** on predictability and who bears usage risk.  
8. Write the passenger **revenue-per-flight** identity; explain why maximising load factor alone can destroy contribution.  
9. Compute **breakeven** under two prices and under two load factors; confront results with capacity.  
10. Run a one-shock **sensitivity** (rent, downtime, or fare) and restate required activity.  
11. List weather loss channels and four response families; name at least one **limitation** of each hedge.  
12. Keep **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**; treat NASA UAM framing and CAAC trial guidance as **comparators / readings**, not HK cost quotes.

Urban air mobility: A comprehensive review and comparative analysis with autonomous and electric ground transportation for informing future research. *Transportation Research Part C*, 132, 103377. doi:10.1016/j.trc.2021.103377](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trc.2021.103377) — Compares UAM with autonomous and electric ground modes; useful for cost and competition benchmarks.

**Official**

English gloss: Guide to trial-operation certification of light/small civil UAS for logistics delivery.

### Looking ahead to Week 4

Week 4 turns to **demand modeling in urban air mobility**. Will customers actually choose an LAE option? We move from potential trips to capacity-limited demand, willingness to pay, and generalized cost — and treat public acceptance as explicit scenarios.

**Preview question:** once you know what you must charge to survive, how do you show that customers might pay it?
